page: Amazon Web Services m8idn.16xlarge is a general-purpose instance built on the AWS Nitro hypervisor architecture, utilizing Intel x86_64 processors. It delivers 64 dedicated vCPUs spanning 32 physical processor cores operating at a 3.9 GHz base clock. The server provides 256 GB of system memory, maintaining a balanced 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio with 4 GB per virtual core. It does not include dedicated graphics processing units.

A key architectural aspect of this configuration is the inclusion of 3,800 GB of integrated local NVMe SSD instance storage alongside a 100 Gbps baseline network bandwidth profile. This direct-attached local storage avoids the latency and throughput constraints of remote network block volumes, while the 100 Gbps network interface provides high-capacity data ingress and egress. Tradeoffs include the ephemeral nature of the local NVMe storage, which requires external data replication or persistent backups for durability.

With its combination of dedicated high-frequency compute, balanced RAM, rapid local storage, and 100 Gbps networking, the m8idn.16xlarge is suited for distributed relational and non-relational databases, large-scale caching tiers, CI/CD pipeline executors, search indexing clusters, and real-time streaming data analytics.
description: Amazon Web Services m8idn.16xlarge is a general-purpose cloud instance powered by 32 physical Intel x86_64 processor cores providing 64 dedicated vCPUs running at 3.9 GHz. Operating under the AWS Nitro hypervisor architecture, it provides a balanced 256 GB of memory, equating to 4 GB per virtual core. Unlike diskless general-purpose variants, the m8idn.16xlarge incorporates 3,800 GB of local NVMe SSD instance storage alongside a 100 Gbps baseline network bandwidth interface. The instance does not feature discrete GPU accelerators. The combination of high clock speed, large memory footprint, fast temporary disk capacity, and wide network pipes provides efficient compute density for workloads that involve heavy input and output operations. Appropriate workload implementations include distributed transactional databases, real-time stream processing, large-scale search engines, and multi-tenant application serving with demanding local I/O requirements.
